paragraphs: A network's loss landscape describes how its errors change as the model changes. Researchers have observed a relationship between the sharpness of that landscape and performance on unseen data. However, conventional sharpness measures can change when the same model is expressed using different parameter coordinates, making their interpretation problematic.

This paper proposes a measure built around the probability distribution represented by the network. Instead of asking how much the loss changes when numerical parameter values move, it asks how the loss changes when the modeled distribution changes. Information geometry supplies the framework for making this distinction. The resulting sharpness measure is invariant to reparametrization, so its value does not depend on the chosen parameter description.

The authors establish theoretical connections between their measure and generalization, and also use it as a training regularizer. Their experiments report significant performance improvements. The contribution therefore combines a more consistent definition of sharpness with evidence that encouraging this property during training can be useful.
neurips-2022-a-reparametrization-invaria.tldr: An information-geometric sharpness measure stays unchanged under reparametrization and improves performance when used as a training regularizer.

paragraphs: Machine learning research in criminal justice often concentrates on a small number of familiar benchmarks, including COMPAS. The paper argues that this attention has not always been accompanied by adequate consideration of domain context. Choosing a dataset requires understanding what it covers and how that coverage relates to the intended research question.

The authors survey publicly available US criminal justice datasets and create datasheets for 15 of them. These documents are placed in a public repository. The survey compares datasets by dimensions including their size, the populations they cover, and their potential uses. It also discusses context, concerns, gaps, and limitations to support more informed selection.

The main contribution is a documented resource for researchers, rather than a new predictive model. Bringing alternatives into view can broaden the starting point for criminal justice and algorithmic fairness studies. The authors present the repository as a resource for responsible use and hope that community contributions will expand it over time.
neurips-2022-a-survey-and-datasheet-repo.tldr: A survey and public repository document 15 criminal justice datasets to help researchers select and use them with better contextual understanding.

paragraphs: Rank aggregation combines voters' comparisons between pairs of items into one overall ordering. This paper studies a setting with two populations: honest voters whose choices follow the Bradley–Terry–Luce score model, and malicious voters who try to corrupt the result. The malicious group can coordinate and knows the underlying scores, honest votes, and ranking algorithm.

The authors show that Rank-Centrality, a spectral method that is optimal under the ordinary score model, can perform poorly even with a small constant fraction of malicious voters. They introduce Byzantine Spectral Ranking and a faster variant. Their method produces a reliable ranking when honest voters outnumber malicious voters, despite the adversary's extensive information.

An accompanying impossibility result shows why the population balance matters: with a malicious majority, no algorithm can give a satisfactory ranking with probability above one half for every possible set of scores. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets support the analysis, demonstrating both Rank-Centrality's vulnerability and the proposed method's robustness under the tested attacks.
neurips-2022-byzantine-spectral-ranking-.tldr: Byzantine Spectral Ranking reliably aggregates adversarial pairwise votes when honest voters form a majority.

paragraphs: Drug recommendation from electronic health records involves more than matching a diagnosis to a medicine. This paper identifies three priorities: addressing recommendation bias caused by limited observable information, using a patient's history across visits, and coordinating multiple drugs with safety in mind. DrugRec brings these priorities into a single recommendation model.

The method uses a causal graph to represent the recommendation process and applies front-door adjustment to identify and remove confounding bias within that model. It also incorporates multiple visits into the graph, allowing historical health conditions to inform recommendations. For combinations of medicines, the authors express drug–drug interactions as a propositional satisfiability problem, so solving logical constraints can help coordinate the selected drugs.

Experiments on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV report state-of-the-art performance, which the authors present as evidence of the method's effectiveness and safety. The significance is the combined treatment of causal bias, longitudinal information, and interactions between recommendations. The reported safety evidence comes from those dataset evaluations of the proposed system.
neurips-2022-debiased-longitudinal-and-c.tldr: DrugRec combines causal adjustment, patient histories, and logical drug-interaction constraints to improve medication recommendations on two clinical datasets.

paragraphs: When several interventions happen together, separating the effect of each one is difficult because the interventions may interact. Hidden factors that influence both treatments and outcomes make this harder. This paper asks whether observational data and records of joint interventions can reveal what a single intervention would do on its own.

The authors first prove that this recovery is not possible in general. They then establish identification results for nonlinear continuous structural causal models with additive, multivariate Gaussian noise. Within this model class, individual intervention effects can be recovered even in the presence of unobserved confounders. The approach also incorporates observed covariates and allows treatment effects to vary across individuals or conditions.

The proofs motivate an algorithm that pools data from different observational and intervention regimes and fits causal model parameters by maximizing their combined likelihood. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate its effectiveness. The key result is a conditional route to separating intervention effects, with the stated structural and noise assumptions providing the basis for identification.
neurips-2022-disentangling-causal-effect.tldr: Under a specified causal model with additive Gaussian noise, pooled observational and joint-intervention data can identify individual intervention effects despite hidden confounders.

paragraphs: Generating a long video requires deciding both what each frame contains and how frames remain consistent over time. This paper presents a video-completion framework based on denoising diffusion models. Its central feature is flexibility: at test time, the model can generate an arbitrary subset of frames while conditioning on any other subset.

The authors develop an architecture that supports this choice of generated and conditioning frames. That capability lets them compare and optimize different schedules for constructing a long video, rather than committing to a single sampling order. It also permits selective use of sparse frames and frames far apart in time as conditioning information, giving the generation process access to earlier content across long intervals.

The paper reports improved video modeling relative to prior work on several datasets and demonstrates temporally coherent samples longer than 25 minutes. It also introduces a video dataset and semantically meaningful evaluation metrics using the CARLA driving simulator. Together, these contributions connect flexible frame generation with long-duration evaluation.
neurips-2022-flexible-diffusion-modeling.tldr: A diffusion model that flexibly chooses generated and conditioning frames produces coherent video samples longer than 25 minutes.

paragraphs: Objects in the same image category can have substantially different shapes, and those differences can carry useful information. Geo-SIC aims to make deformable geometry an explicit part of image classification. The paper addresses the tendency for shape information to remain implicit or underused in image analysis models.

The framework learns features from both the image and a latent space describing shape variation. Its classifier is coupled to unsupervised learning of geometric representations, with within-class shape changes characterized by diffeomorphic transformations. Rather than requiring shapes to be extracted beforehand, it learns relevant shape features jointly with the classification task. This gives the model access to appearance and geometry while accommodating large variations within a category.

Experiments on simulated two-dimensional images and real three-dimensional brain MR images report substantial improvements in classification accuracy. The authors also report increased interpretability because the learned geometric features can be accessed directly. The contribution is therefore both a classification method and a way to expose shape information underlying its image representations.
neurips-2022-geo-sic-learning-deformable.tldr: Geo-SIC jointly learns image and deformable-shape features, improving classification accuracy and access to interpretable geometry in its experiments.

paragraphs: Hedging is usually associated with financial contracts, but the paper treats it as a broader decision problem. An agent may care about uncertain outcomes whose value is not monetary. For a risk-averse agent, a useful opportunity can arise when an additional reward helps balance the uncertain rewards already present in its situation.

The authors formalize this idea by adding a reward to a probabilistic graphical model, specifically a Bayesian network or an influence diagram. Hedging then becomes a particular operation on a graph representing uncertainty and decisions. This puts it alongside analyses of interventions and information gathering, while focusing on how rewards can be combined to manage uncertainty.

The paper develops examples and counter-examples to clarify the proposed concept and experiments to examine its computational tools. Those tools are intended to help agents actively identify potential hedging opportunities. The contribution is a general decision-theoretic formulation, together with demonstrations of its properties and applicability beyond the exclusively financial interpretation of hedging.
neurips-2022-hedging-as-reward-augmentat.tldr: The paper models hedging as adding rewards to probabilistic graphs so risk-averse agents can identify opportunities to balance uncertain outcomes.

paragraphs: A model zoo contains multiple trained neural networks, each represented by its weights. Earlier work used an autoencoder to learn a hyper-representation of such collections, capturing properties of the networks. This paper extends that idea from representing existing models to generating new sets of weights.

The authors introduce layer-wise loss normalization, which they demonstrate is important for producing high-performing models. They also develop several sampling methods that use the topology of the learned hyper-representation. The aim is to draw useful new models from the structure learned across the collection, turning a representation of network weights into a generative resource.

The generated networks are evaluated for initialization, ensemble sampling, and transfer learning. Across these downstream tasks, the authors report diverse, capable models that can outperform strong baselines. The results suggest that information distributed across a model zoo can be aggregated into new networks through hyper-representations. This is evidence for the generative potential of learned weight spaces, rather than only their usefulness for inspecting existing models.
neurips-2022-hyper-representations-as-ge.tldr: Learned representations of model collections can generate diverse new network weights useful for initialization, ensembles, and transfer learning.

paragraphs: Multi-head attention gives a transformer multiple attention matrices, but computing and storing those matrices can be expensive. This paper builds on the observation that attention matrices occupy a low-dimensional manifold and therefore contain redundancy. FiSHformers aim to exploit that redundancy by allowing different attention heads to share matrices.

The central mechanism is a finite admixture model of shared heads. It samples attention matrices from a collection of global attention matrices that is much smaller than the number of local matrices produced. The transformer learns those global matrices directly. Sharing this smaller collection reduces the amount of distinct attention structure that the model must learn and maintain.

The authors evaluate the approach on language modeling, machine translation, and image classification, reporting advantages over baseline transformers. On WikiText-103, IWSLT'14 De-En, and WMT'14 En-De, FiSHformers require substantially less computation, memory, and fewer parameters. The results support attention sharing as a practical way to improve efficiency while retaining a flexible transformer architecture.
neurips-2022-improving-transformer-with-.tldr: FiSHformers share a small collection of learned attention matrices across heads to reduce transformer computation, memory use, and parameter counts.

paragraphs: MATE is a simulated environment for studying groups of learning agents with both cooperative and competitive goals. One team controls directional cameras and tries to maximize coverage of moving targets. The other team transports cargo between randomly assigned warehouses while trying to minimize exposure to those cameras.

The teams have different capabilities and objectives, creating an asymmetric game. The authors use this setting to examine cooperation, communication, scalability, robustness, and self-play. They benchmark several multi-agent reinforcement learning methods, add communication protocols, and evaluate self-play techniques in the zero-sum competition between cameras and targets. The environment therefore supports several related research questions within one task structure.

The paper reports that co-evolution through self-play helps produce a camera network that is less exploitable. It also observes distinct roles emerging among target agents when they communicate using I2C. MATE is implemented in Python and integrates with the OpenAI Gym interface. Its contribution combines a reusable benchmark with evidence about communication and competitive training in target coverage.
neurips-2022-mate-benchmarking-multi-age.tldr: MATE benchmarks multi-agent learning through competing camera and cargo-transport teams, revealing benefits from communication and self-play.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether the strategy of scaling transformers on diverse datasets can also produce generalist reinforcement learning agents. The goal is a single agent that can use experience from many tasks, rather than requiring a separate set of model weights for each game.

The authors train one transformer entirely offline and show that a single set of weights can support play across a suite of up to 46 Atari games at close-to-human performance. They compare Multi-Game Decision Transformers with online and offline reinforcement learning approaches and behavioral cloning in this shared multi-game setting. Their models offer the best scalability and performance among the approaches evaluated.

With appropriate training and evaluation, the study finds that performance improves with model size and that fine-tuning allows rapid adaptation to new games. These findings echo trends seen in language and vision within the tested setting. The release of pretrained models and code supports further investigation of learning broadly capable agents from diverse, previously collected experience.
neurips-2022-multi-game-decision-transfo.tldr: A single offline-trained transformer plays up to 46 Atari games at close-to-human performance and benefits from scaling and fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search needs efficient ways to predict which candidate networks will perform well. Zero-cost proxies provide inexpensive performance signals, but their biases and complementary strengths have received less study. This paper creates a shared dataset and codebase to make those questions easier to investigate consistently.

The resource evaluates 13 proxies across 28 tasks. Reusing these results enables experiments that are orders of magnitude faster, while a unified implementation reduces confounding differences between codebases. The authors use the resource for a large-scale bias study and an information-theoretic analysis. The latter finds that different proxies contain substantial complementary information, making their combination potentially valuable.

Based on this analysis, the paper proposes reducing proxy biases such as those associated with cell size. It also incorporates all 13 proxies into the surrogate models used by architecture-search algorithms, reporting predictive performance improvements of up to 42%. The contribution links benchmarking infrastructure to concrete methods for obtaining more useful architecture-performance predictions.
neurips-2022-nas-bench-suite-zero-accele.tldr: A unified benchmark of 13 zero-cost proxies across 28 tasks reveals complementary signals that can improve architecture-performance prediction.

paragraphs: Non-rigid point cloud registration aligns three-dimensional point sets when the underlying object can deform. Unlike a single rigid movement, deformation can involve complex changes across different parts of the object. Neural Deformation Pyramid addresses this complexity by breaking the unknown motion into a hierarchy of smaller motion updates.

Each level of the pyramid uses a multilayer perceptron that receives a sinusoidally encoded three-dimensional point and predicts an increment to the motion from the preceding level. The encoding begins at low frequency and increases through the hierarchy. This produces a staged decomposition from rigid to non-rigid motion, allowing successive levels to represent increasingly detailed changes.

The authors report a 50-fold solving speedup compared with an existing MLP-based approach. They also report strong partial-to-partial registration results on 4DMatch and 4DLoMatch under both no-learned and supervised settings. The central contribution is a structured representation of deformation that improves solving efficiency while handling the alignment of incomplete point clouds.
neurips-2022-non-rigid-point-cloud-regis.tldr: Neural Deformation Pyramid decomposes point-cloud motion hierarchically, reporting strong registration results and a 50-fold speedup over an existing MLP approach.

paragraphs: Generalization concerns how well a model handles unseen data, while invariance concerns whether its predictions stay consistent when inputs are transformed. This paper quantitatively investigates the relationship between these properties. It focuses on image rotation and grayscale conversion, rather than treating invariance as an unspecified property.

The authors introduce effective invariance, a measure that does not require image labels. It compares a model's predictions for an image and its transformed version, accounting for both agreement and confidence. This provides a way to measure prediction consistency directly from model outputs and then study how that consistency relates to accuracy.

Large-scale experiments reveal a strong linear relationship across different models between generalization and measured invariance, on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution datasets. Looking across test sets for a fixed model also reveals a linear correlation between accuracy and invariance. These findings give quantitative support to the proposed relationship in the studied settings; they establish correlation rather than showing that increasing invariance necessarily causes better generalization.
neurips-2022-on-the-strong-correlation-b.tldr: A label-free measure of prediction invariance shows strong linear correlations with generalization across models and test datasets.

paragraphs: Simulating plastic materials poses a difficulty for methods built around energy optimization. Elastic forces such as spring forces can be derived from a potential energy, but the plastic forces considered here do not arise from a positional energy gradient. That mismatch complicates the stability and flexibility of simulations involving materials such as metal, sand, and snow.

PlasticityNet learns a generalizable plastic energy whose derivative closely approximates the analytical behavior of the plastic forces. The learned energy supplies a representation that can be used by optimization-based time integration. This connects material behavior that is difficult to express in the required energy form with an integration framework designed around that form.

The authors report that the approach enables a broad range of elasticity–plasticity combinations using time-step-independent, unconditionally stable optimization-based integrators. They demonstrate challenging two- and three-dimensional effects involving metal, sand, and snow with complex dynamics. The contribution is the learned energy representation that makes these material combinations accessible to the stated stable integration methods.
neurips-2022-plasticitynet-learning-to-s.tldr: PlasticityNet learns an energy representation of plastic forces that enables stable optimization-based simulations of materials including metal, sand, and snow.

paragraphs: This paper studies what single-qubit quantum neural networks can represent. It focuses on data re-uploading networks, which alternate circuit blocks that encode inputs with blocks containing trainable parameters. The question is about expressive ability: which functions such circuits can approximate and where their representational limits arise.

For functions of one variable, the authors establish universal approximation by relating the network to a partial Fourier series. They derive exact relationships between trainable gate parameters and Fourier coefficients. This makes the connection between circuit choices and the resulting function explicit, resolving an open question about the approximation capability of these networks.

The analysis then examines functions of multiple variables, where the available frequency spectrum and freedom to adjust Fourier coefficients impose limitations on single-qubit native networks. Numerical experiments demonstrate both expressive power and constraints. The results distinguish the strong univariate approximation finding from the more restricted multivariate case and provide theoretical guidance for designing quantum neural networks.
neurips-2022-power-and-limitations-of-si.tldr: Fourier analysis establishes single-qubit networks' univariate approximation power while exposing limitations for functions of multiple variables.

paragraphs: Regularization methods depend on coefficients that control how strongly fitting is constrained. This paper studies how to tune those coefficients across multiple problem instances for Ridge regression, LASSO, and ElasticNet. The setting includes cross-validation and hyperparameter optimization across tasks, with the aim of providing learning-theoretic guarantees for tuning.

The central mathematical result describes ElasticNet loss as a piecewise-rational function of its tuning parameters, with algebraic boundaries separating the pieces. This structure lets the authors bound the complexity of the family of loss functions. They use those bounds to establish statistical generalization guarantees for choosing regularization coefficients.

The paper also treats online tuning, proving that average expected regret relative to the best parameter pair vanishes. It extends the analysis to classifiers formed by thresholding regularized regression predictions. The guarantees cover validation objectives and popular information criteria while avoiding strong assumptions about the data distribution. The contribution explains why tuning across instances can be learnable, rather than merely providing another parameter-search procedure.
neurips-2022-provably-tuning-the-elastic.tldr: A structural analysis of ElasticNet loss yields statistical and online guarantees for tuning regularization across problem instances.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning infers a cost function that explains an expert's behavior. RHIRL targets continuous systems with many dimensions, noisy demonstrations, and black-box dynamics. Its design addresses the difficulty of matching expert behavior across an entire high-dimensional state space while remaining robust to imperfections in the data and control process.

The algorithm compares its induced optimal trajectories with expert demonstrations over local, receding horizons. It then combines those local solutions to learn the cost. This local construction avoids the global matching approach used by earlier methods and is the paper's route around the curse of dimensionality. Under mild conditions, RHIRL also learns a state-dependent cost disentangled from system dynamics.

Benchmark experiments show that RHIRL outperforms several leading inverse reinforcement learning algorithms in most tested instances. The authors additionally prove that its cumulative error grows linearly with task duration. Together, these findings connect the method's local construction to practical performance and an explicit characterization of how error accumulates over time.
neurips-2022-receding-horizon-inverse-re.tldr: RHIRL learns costs from local trajectory matches, improving scalability and robustness while guaranteeing linear cumulative-error growth with task duration.

paragraphs: This paper develops a model that discovers, tracks, and segments multiple moving objects in video. Its representation assigns objects to depth-ordered layers, making the ordering of overlapping objects part of the model. A transformer variant processes optical flow, with each query representing an object and its layer throughout the video.

The authors also build a scalable synthetic-data pipeline by composing multiple object layers. Training on this data reduces the need for labor-intensive annotations and supports transfer from synthetic scenes to real videos. Ablation studies show that the model can learn object permanence and temporal shape consistency, and predict amodal masks that include portions of objects hidden by occlusion.

Trained only on synthetic data, the model achieves state-of-the-art results among methods that use no manual annotations on DAVIS, MoCA, SegTrack, and FBMS-59. Test-time adaptation provides further improvements. The findings connect an explicit layered object representation with effective handling of mutual occlusion and transfer to standard video segmentation benchmarks.
neurips-2022-segmenting-moving-objects-v.tldr: A depth-layered transformer trained on synthetic videos tracks and segments moving objects, including hidden regions, without manual training annotations.

paragraphs: Sometimes predictions must be made without a labeled training set, using only existing expert models and limited information about their original training data. Those data may remain private even when the models are shared. This paper asks how to combine such models when their experience covers different parts of the input space.

The proposed method assigns ensemble weights separately for each test instance. Its guiding idea is to give more influence to models whose training domains are more relevant to that particular instance. This differs from selecting one model or one global combination for every input. The method also includes a representation-learning step designed for sparse, high-dimensional domains.

The authors demonstrate the approach on classical machine learning tasks and a real-world application involving vancomycin precision dosing. These evaluations support the usefulness and generalizability of instance-wise combination. The contribution is a way to use a collection of privately trained experts while recognizing that the most relevant expert can change from one prediction to the next.
neurips-2022-synthetic-model-combination.tldr: Synthetic Model Combination weights expert models separately for each input using their domain relevance, without requiring a labeled training set.

paragraphs: Virtual screening compares candidate compounds with known active ligands to prioritize molecules likely to bind a target. ToDD approaches this as a topology-based graph-ranking problem. The motivation is to improve compound representations beyond established fingerprints and learned alternatives whose performance can decline on large virtual compound collections.

The method partitions a compound into chemical substructures using periodic properties of its atoms. It then extracts persistent homology features at multiple resolutions using multiparameter persistence, producing multidimensional topological fingerprints. Pretrained triplet networks are fine-tuned with a margin loss to distinguish compounds in an embedding space and support candidate ranking.

The authors prove stability properties for their proposed signatures and report strong benchmark improvements when models incorporate them. Reported gains include 93% on Cleves-Jain and 54% on DUD-E Diverse, with highly statistically significant margins over state-of-the-art methods. These are virtual-screening benchmark findings: the contribution is a stable representation and ranking approach for prioritizing candidates, with empirical evidence that the topological information improves the tested models.
neurips-2022-todd-topological-compound-f.tldr: ToDD uses stable topological compound fingerprints to improve virtual-screening rankings, reporting substantial gains on two named benchmarks.

paragraphs: An untargeted graph-structure attack changes graph edges to degrade node classification. With a limited perturbation budget, the attack objective determines which changes appear most valuable. This paper questions the common use of negative cross-entropy, arguing that its gradients can direct resources toward nodes that are already misclassified.

The authors demonstrate theoretically and empirically that this objective tends to produce larger gradients for nodes with lower confidence in their labeled classes. That tendency can persist even after a node's prediction has been misled. Consequently, gradient magnitude may encourage further spending on an already affected node instead of using the remaining budget more effectively.

The proposed attack uses a new objective that produces unweighted graph-structure gradients unaffected by node confidence. Experiments in gray-box poisoning scenarios show that this change in budget allocation can significantly improve the effectiveness of gradient-based edge perturbations without adding a hyperparameter. The contribution links a specific bias in the objective to inefficient resource allocation and provides a simple corrective alternative.
neurips-2022-towards-reasonable-budget-a.tldr: A confidence-independent attack objective improves graph-edge perturbation budgets by reducing attention to nodes that are already misclassified.

paragraphs: Increasing a language model's size does not automatically make its responses match a user's intent. This paper investigates a training process that uses human feedback to improve instruction following. It starts from GPT-3 and gathers prompts written by labelers as well as prompts submitted through a language-model API.

The process has two stages. First, human demonstrations of desired responses provide supervised training examples. Second, rankings of model outputs guide further training through reinforcement learning from human feedback. The resulting models are called InstructGPT. The demonstrations show the model what desired behavior looks like, while the rankings provide comparative judgments about generated answers.

On the evaluated prompt distribution, human evaluators prefer the 1.3-billion-parameter InstructGPT model's outputs to those of the 175-billion-parameter GPT-3. InstructGPT also improves truthfulness and reduces toxic output, with minimal regressions on public NLP datasets. It still makes simple mistakes, but the results show that feedback-based fine-tuning can improve alignment with user intent without relying solely on greater model size.
neurips-2022-training-language-models-to.tldr: Human demonstrations and preference feedback make InstructGPT better at following user intent, with evaluators preferring a much smaller model on the tested prompts.

paragraphs: A self-driving car's object detector must work in environments different from those used for training. Unlabeled data from a new environment can support adaptation, but it lacks a reliable supervisory signal. This paper adds a specific assumption: the available data include multiple traversals of the same routes, providing repeated observations of shared locations.

The method starts with pseudo-labels generated by an out-of-domain detector. It compares observations across traversals and removes detections of supposedly mobile objects that remain persistent, reducing false positives. It also encourages detections in nonpersistent regions to reduce false negatives. These corrections supply a signal for iteratively retraining the detector on the target environment.

Experiments on two large driving datasets report substantial improvements in detecting cars, pedestrians, and cyclists. The key finding is that repeated route observations can provide sufficient additional structure for useful self-training without new annotations. The approach's adaptation signal depends on the availability of those repeated traversals, which the authors argue is realistic because many drivers use the same roads.
neurips-2022-unsupervised-adaptation-fro.tldr: Repeated drives along the same routes provide signals that improve pseudo-labels and adapt 3D object detectors without new annotations.
